quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on hank prices, thread-weighted averages and the four steps of costing a yarn mixture.

questions.q: The first step in costing a yarn mixture is to convert each price per 10 lb into:
questions.explain: Hank price = price ÷ 10 ÷ Ne puts every yarn on a common length basis (one 840-yd hank), which is what threads actually consume.

questions.q: The mean hank price is weighted by:
options: The number of threads of each yarn
The weight in pounds of each yarn
questions.explain: Mean hank price = Σ(threads × hank price) ÷ Σ threads: each thread consumes one hank per hank-length, so threads are the right weights.

questions.q: Which Excel function does the lecture name for Σ(threads × hank price)?
questions.explain: SUMPRODUCT multiplies the threads column by the hank-price column pair by pair and adds the products in one step.

questions.q: The mean count in this lecture is found:
options: Exactly as in Lecture 3, Σ threads ÷ Σ(threads ÷ Ne)
questions.explain: Step 3 is the Lecture 3 proportion formula; price does not enter the count calculation.

questions.q: The price of the mixture per 10 lb equals mean hank price × mean count × 10.
questions.explain: Mean count is hanks per pound of the mixture; multiplying by the mean hank price gives the price per pound, and × 10 gives the price per 10 lb.

questions.q: In the worksheet, yarn C has a hank price of Rs 2.15 but contributes Rs 0.00 to the threads × hank column. Why?
options: Its threads are set to 0, so it is an unused slot
questions.explain: Hank price is calculated from count and price alone, but with 0 threads the product threads × hank is 0 and the slot adds nothing.

questions.q: When all yarns in the mix have the same count, the price of the mixture is:
options: The simple average of the prices per 10 lb
The thread-weighted average of the prices per 10 lb
questions.explain: With equal counts the hank-price route reduces to a thread-weighted average of the prices per 10 lb: 511.04 for 56 threads at 515 and 4.35 at 460.

questions.q: A hank price depends on which two inputs?
questions.explain: Hank price = price per 10 lb ÷ 10 ÷ Ne; the number of threads only enters later as a weight.

questions.q: Changing one yarn to a coarser count at a different price moves both the mean count and the mixture price.
questions.explain: The lecture's hint (change yarn C to 10 threads of Ne 20 at Rs 430) shows count and price moving together, since both depend on threads ÷ Ne and threads × hank price.

questions.q: Why is the price not simply averaged per 10 lb when counts differ?
options: Because 10 lb of a fine yarn contains more length than 10 lb of a coarse yarn, so equal weights are not equal thread contributions
Because Ne is a direct system
questions.explain: Threads consume length, not weight; hank prices put the yarns on a length basis before weighting by threads.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: The four formulas of the costing worksheet and how the result responds when a price, a count or a thread number changes.

questions.q: Hank price is calculated as:
questions.explain: Divide by 10 for the price per pound, then by Ne (hanks per pound) for the price per hank: Rs 515 ÷ 10 ÷ 30 = Rs 1.7167.

questions.q: Mean hank price is:
options: Σ hank prices ÷ number of yarns
questions.explain: The thread-weighted average; the simple average of hank prices (first option) is Lecture 2's equal-share case and is wrong when thread numbers differ.

questions.q: If every price per 10 lb rises by 5 % and nothing else changes, the mixture price per 10 lb:
questions.explain: Every hank price rises 5 %, so the mean hank price rises 5 %; mean count is unchanged, so the product rises 5 %.

questions.q: Increasing the number of threads of the cheaper yarn (same count) will:
options: Lower the mean hank price and the mixture price
questions.explain: More weight on a lower hank price pulls the mean hank price down; with equal counts the mean count stays put, so the mixture price falls.

questions.q: For a yarn of fixed price per 10 lb, the hank price falls as its Ne rises.
questions.explain: A finer yarn has more hanks per pound, so each hank costs less: Rs 430 at Ne 20 gives Rs 2.15 per hank, but at Ne 40 it would give Rs 1.075.

questions.q: Which quantity does SUMPRODUCT(threads, hank price) produce in the worksheet?
options: The total of column F, Rs 102.80
questions.explain: SUMPRODUCT gives Σ(threads × hank price) = 96.13 + 6.67 = 102.80; dividing by Σ threads (60.35) then gives the mean hank price 1.7035.

questions.q: In the final step, why multiply the mean hank price by the mean count?
options: To convert from hanks to pounds, since mean count is hanks per pound
questions.explain: A pound of the mixture contains mean-count hanks, so price per pound = mean hank price × mean count; × 10 then gives the price per 10 lb.

questions.q: Replacing yarn B (4.35 threads of Ne 30 at Rs 460) with the same threads of Ne 30 at Rs 515 would make the mixture price:
questions.explain: All threads would then be Ne 30 at Rs 515, so the thread-weighted price is simply Rs 515.

questions.q: The mean count of the mixture depends on the prices entered.
questions.explain: Mean count uses only counts and threads (Σ threads ÷ Σ(threads ÷ Ne)); prices affect only the hank price and the final mixture price.

questions.q: Doubling the number of threads of every yarn in the worksheet (same counts, same prices) changes the mixture price per 10 lb by:
questions.explain: Both Σ(threads × hank) and Σ threads double, so the mean hank price is unchanged; the mean count is unchanged for the same reason, so the price per 10 lb stays the same.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Hank prices, SUMPRODUCT totals and mixture prices from the worksheet figures and from new realistic ones.

questions.q: Ne 30 yarn costs Rs 515 per 10 lb. Hank price, to four decimal places?
questions.explain: 515 ÷ 10 = 51.5 per lb; ÷ 30 hanks per lb = Rs 1.7167 per hank.

questions.q: Ne 20 yarn costs Rs 430 per 10 lb. Hank price, to two decimal places?
questions.explain: 430 ÷ 10 ÷ 20 = Rs 2.15 per hank — the yarn C figure in the worksheet.

questions.q: Yarn A has 56 threads at a hank price of Rs 1.7167. What is threads × hank price, to two decimal places?
questions.explain: 56 × 1.7167 = 96.13, the first entry in column F.

questions.q: Σ(threads × hank) = Rs 102.80 and Σ threads = 60.35. Mean hank price, to four decimal places?
Mean hank price Rs 1.7035 and mean count Ne 30. Price of the mixture per 10 lb, to the nearest rupee?
questions.explain: 1.7035 × 30 × 10 = Rs 511.05 ≈ Rs 511, matching the worksheet's 511.04.

questions.q: A warp uses 50 threads of Ne 20 at Rs 400/10 lb and 50 threads of Ne 40 at Rs 900/10 lb. Mean hank price, to three decimal places?
questions.explain: Hank prices 2.00 and 2.25; equal threads, so the mean is (2.00 + 2.25) ÷ 2 = Rs 2.125.

questions.q: For the same warp (50 × Ne 20, 50 × Ne 40), what is the mean count, to two decimal places?
With mean hank price Rs 2.125 and mean count Ne 26.67, what is the price of the mixture per 10 lb, to the nearest rupee?
questions.explain: 2.125 × 26.67 × 10 = Rs 566.7 ≈ Rs 567 per 10 lb — between the Rs 400 and Rs 900 of the two yarns but nearer the coarse one, which carries more weight.

questions.q: 56 threads at Rs 515 and 4.35 threads at Rs 460, both Ne 30. The thread-weighted price per 10 lb is:
questions.explain: (56 × 515 + 4.35 × 460) ÷ 60.35 = 30,841 ÷ 60.35 = Rs 511.04. Rs 487.50 is the unweighted average of the two prices.

questions.q: A Ne 60 yarn costs Rs 1,200 per 10 lb. Its hank price is:
questions.explain: 1,200 ÷ 10 ÷ 60 = Rs 2.00 per hank. Rs 20 forgets to divide by 10 and Rs 7.20 would be 1,200 × 6 ÷ 1,000.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Costing-office decisions: pricing striped warps, comparing yarn offers and spotting what a wrong average does to a quotation.

questions.q: A stripe warp is 56 threads of Ne 30 at Rs 515 and 4.35 threads of Ne 30 at Rs 460 (dyed). The merchandiser quotes yarn at Rs 487.50 per 10 lb (the average of the two). What is wrong?
options: The prices must be thread-weighted: the correct figure is Rs 511.04, so the quote is about Rs 23.50 too low
The quote should be Rs 515 because the dyed yarn is negligible
The quote should be Rs 460 because dyed yarn is cheaper
questions.explain: Only 7 % of the threads are at Rs 460, so the weighted price is 511.04; an unweighted average undercharges by Rs 23.56 per 10 lb.

questions.q: You add 10 threads of Ne 20 at Rs 430 to the default warp (as the lecture suggests). What happens to mean count and price per 10 lb?
options: Count falls to about Ne 28 and price falls to about Rs 495
Count falls and price rises above Rs 515
questions.explain: Σ threads 70.35, Σ(threads ÷ Ne) 2.5117 → Ne 28.01; Σ(threads × hank) 124.30 → mean hank 1.7669; price = 1.7669 × 28.01 × 10 = Rs 494.9.

questions.q: Two offers for a plain warp: Ne 30 at Rs 515 per 10 lb, or Ne 40 at Rs 650 per 10 lb. Which gives the cheaper hank, and by how much?
options: Ne 30, cheaper by Rs 0.09 per hank
Ne 40, cheaper by Rs 0.09 per hank
Both cost the same per hank
Ne 40, cheaper by Rs 1.35 per hank
questions.explain: Ne 30: 515 ÷ 300 = Rs 1.717; Ne 40: 650 ÷ 400 = Rs 1.625. The finer yarn costs more per pound but Rs 0.09 less per hank of length.

questions.q: If a fabric needs a fixed number of ends and length, comparing yarn offers by hank price is more relevant than comparing by price per 10 lb.
questions.explain: The warp consumes length (ends × warp length), so the cost of that length — hanks × hank price — is what matters; price per pound alone ignores how much length a pound gives.

questions.q: The dyed-yarn supplier raises yarn B from Rs 460 to Rs 560 per 10 lb (4.35 of 60.35 threads). The mixture price rises by about:
questions.explain: With equal counts the price is thread-weighted: 4.35 ÷ 60.35 × 100 = Rs 7.2 per 10 lb. The small share of threads limits the impact.

questions.q: Your sheet shows a mixture price higher than every individual price per 10 lb. What is the likely error?
options: Prices were entered in Rs per lb
The mean count was multiplied instead of divided somewhere, or threads and counts were swapped
questions.explain: A weighted mixture price must lie between the lowest and highest yarn prices; an out-of-range result means an input or formula error — check the hank-price division and the count column.

questions.q: A towel mill runs 2,400 pile ends of Ne 16 at Rs 480/10 lb and 1,200 ground ends of Ne 24 at Rs 540/10 lb. Which figure goes into the threads × hank column for the pile?
questions.explain: Pile hank price = 480 ÷ 10 ÷ 16 = Rs 3.00; threads × hank = 2,400 × 3.00 = 7,200. 2,400 ÷ 16 belongs to the count column, not the price column.

questions.q: Yarn prices are quoted per 10 lb, but the warp length is planned in hanks. Which single number lets you cost the warp directly?
options: The price of the most used yarn
questions.explain: Total yarn cost = total hanks consumed × mean hank price; the mean count is only needed to convert back to a weight-based price.

questions.q: A buyer asks for the fabric with cheaper yarn. Replacing 10 of the 56 Ne 30 threads (Rs 515) with Ne 20 threads at Rs 430 lowers the price per 10 lb. Does it also lower the cost of a given warp length?
options: Yes — a lower price per 10 lb always means lower total cost
Not necessarily: Ne 20 hanks cost Rs 2.15 against Rs 1.72, so each replaced end costs more per hank-length
questions.explain: Price per 10 lb falls because the mixture gets heavier (lower mean count), but the hank price of Ne 20 is higher, so the cost of the same length of warp rises.

questions.q: A trainee leaves the threads of yarn C at 0 but enters a price. The mixture price is unaffected. Is that correct behaviour?
options: Yes — an unused slot with 0 threads contributes nothing to either total
No — any price entered must change the result
No — the sheet should show an error
Yes, but only if the count is also 0
questions.explain: threads × hank and threads ÷ Ne are both 0 when threads are 0, so the slot is idle; this is how the four-slot worksheet is meant to be used.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Full worksheet runs and reverse problems that combine Lectures 2, 3 and 4 — mean count, mean hank price and mixture price together.

questions.q: Warp: 56 threads Ne 30 at Rs 515, 4.35 threads Ne 30 at Rs 460, 10 threads Ne 20 at Rs 430 (prices per 10 lb). Mean count, to two decimal places?
For the same warp (56 × Ne 30 @ 515, 4.35 × Ne 30 @ 460, 10 × Ne 20 @ 430), mean hank price to four decimal places?
With mean hank price Rs 1.7669 and mean count Ne 28.01, the price of the mixture per 10 lb to the nearest rupee is:
questions.explain: 1.7669 × 28.01 × 10 = Rs 494.9 ≈ Rs 495 per 10 lb, down from Rs 511 before the coarse yarn was added.

questions.q: In the three-yarn warp above the price per 10 lb fell from 511 to 495, yet the coarse yarn has the highest hank price (2.15). Which explanation is right?
options: Per pound the mix is now coarser (fewer hanks per pound), so the weight-based price falls even though the length-based price rose
Cheaper yarn always lowers every price
questions.explain: Mean hank price rose 1.7035 → 1.7669, but mean count fell 30 → 28.01; the product fell because the drop in hanks per pound outweighed the rise in hank price.

questions.q: A spinner's hank price is Rs 1.625 for Ne 40. What is the price per 10 lb?
questions.explain: Reverse the hank-price formula: 1.625 × 40 × 10 = Rs 650 per 10 lb.

questions.q: If two yarns have the same hank price, the mixture's hank price is that value whatever the thread proportions.
questions.explain: A thread-weighted average of equal values is that value; only the mean count (and so the price per 10 lb) would vary with the proportions if the counts differ.

questions.q: A mixture must be sold at Rs 600 per 10 lb and has a mean count of Ne 24. What mean hank price does that imply, to two decimal places?
questions.explain: Mean hank price = price ÷ 10 ÷ mean count = 600 ÷ 10 ÷ 24 = Rs 2.50.

questions.q: Yarn A (Ne 20, Rs 2.00 per hank) and yarn B (Ne 40, Rs 2.25 per hank) in equal threads give a mixture at Rs 567 per 10 lb. If B's threads are doubled, the mixture price per 10 lb will:
options: Rise, because the mean hank price and mean count both rise
Fall, because B costs more per hank
questions.explain: Mean hank price → (2.00 + 2 × 2.25) ÷ 3 = 2.167; mean count → 150 ÷ (2.5 + 2.5) = 30; price = 2.167 × 30 × 10 = Rs 650. Both factors rise.

questions.q: A warp of 3,600 ends is 2,000 yd long. At a mean hank price of Rs 1.7035, what is the warp yarn cost to the nearest rupee? (1 hank = 840 yd.)
Which sequence is the correct order of the four costing steps?
options: Price per 10 lb → mean count → hank price → mean hank price
Hank price → mean hank price → mean count → price per 10 lb
Mean hank price → hank price → price per 10 lb → mean count
Mean hank price → hank price → mean count → price per 10 lb
questions.explain: The lecture lists: convert each price to a hank price, weight the hank prices by threads (SUMPRODUCT), find the mean count as in Lecture 3, then multiply mean hank price × mean count × 10. Mean hank price cannot come before the hank prices, and the final price needs both means.
